platform.value: ISS (Microgravity Science Glovebox / MSG, Destiny laboratory)

sources.note: NASA ISS experiment page: SAME was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the ISS during Expedition 15 and reflown on Expeditions 23/24.
Challenge brief: fire detection was tested in microgravity through SAME and SAME-R.

objective.value: Characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low gravity by overheated spacecraft materials, in order to evaluate and improve spacecraft smoke detectors.

sources.note: SAME final report (NASA TM, NIST): characterize smoke particle size distribution from overheated spacecraft materials; develop the moment method; assess ISS and Shuttle detector performance.
NASA: SAME measures the size distribution of smoke particles to support smoke-detection requirements and improve future spacecraft detectors.
NASA SAME one-pager: assess size/distribution of smoke particles from spacecraft materials and evaluate ionization and photoelectric detector performance.

NASA: crew pyrolyzed solid spacecraft materials (Kapton, silicone rubber, Teflon, cellulose lamp wick) plus a liquid baseline material, dibutyl-phthalate.
SAME final report: four solid materials plus a fifth liquid reference material, dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) retained in a cotton wick.

fuel_phase.note: Samples were heated below the ignition point (oxidative pyrolysis), not burned as a flame. Both solid polymers and a liquid reference material were tested, so the phase is recorded as mixed.

sources.note: SAME final report: samples supported and heated by the same stainless-steel wire coil, six pre-weighed samples per carousel; DBP held on a wick.
NIST/NASA: samples wrapped in wire filaments and loaded into a rotatable carousel; current applied to the wires heats the materials to produce smoke.

NASA news: the MPASS two-moment sensor was flown on the SAME reflight.

relevance_notes.value: SAME is the microgravity fire-detection study named in the challenge brief. Its key finding for fire safety is that the ISS light-scattering detector missed the smallest smoke particles (from Kapton and Teflon), showing that current single-moment spacecraft detectors are not sensitive to all relevant smoke types.

sources.note: Challenge brief: fire detection was tested in microgravity through the SAME and SAME-R studies.
NIST/NASA: the ISS detector failed to detect the smaller Teflon and Kapton smoke particles; no single current method detects all smoke sizes.

value: smoke detectors for other extreme/confined environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories
more nuisance-free (false-alarm-resistant) smoke detectors for homes and buildings
portable real-time particulate sensor (MPASS) for first responders and air-quality monitoring in mines and factories

sources.note: NASA: smoke detectors developed from SAME results can be useful in other extreme environments on Earth such as submarines or underwater laboratories.
NASA news: better nuisance-free detectors for homes; the small MPASS sensor could help first responders and measure particles in mines and factories.
